reference.source: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry; DSM-5-TR
clinicalPearls: The defining feature is marked, persistent fear of one or more social or performance situations in which the person feels exposed to possible scrutiny, with fear of acting in a way that will be humiliating or negatively judged
Feared situations are avoided or endured with intense distress, and the anxiety is out of proportion to any real threat and typically lasts many months
A performance-only subtype exists, confined to situations such as public speaking, and often responds well to targeted strategies
Onset is usually in childhood or adolescence, and the disorder is frequently underrecognised because sufferers are quiet and avoidant rather than disruptive
Comorbidity with depression, other anxiety disorders, and alcohol misuse is common, and alcohol is often used as maladaptive self-medication
First-line treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy with graded exposure and cognitive restructuring, with SSRIs or SNRIs as effective pharmacological options
For circumscribed performance anxiety, beta-adrenergic blockade can dampen peripheral symptoms such as tremor and palpitations, used situationally rather than daily
Distinguish from normal shyness by the degree of distress, avoidance, and functional impairment it causes
reference.pathophysiology: Social anxiety disorder reflects an interaction between heritable temperamental traits, notably behavioural inhibition in early childhood, and altered function of fear and threat-appraisal circuits involving the amygdala and prefrontal cortex. Dysregulation of serotonergic and dopaminergic systems, heightened sensitivity to social evaluation, and learned avoidance that prevents disconfirmation of feared outcomes together maintain the condition.
additionalDifferentials: Panic disorder with or without agoraphobia
Autism spectrum disorder with social difficulties
Major depressive disorder with social withdrawal
Body dysmorphic disorder driving social avoidance
additionalInvestigations: Structured clinical interview focusing on feared and avoided situations
Standardised social anxiety rating scales to gauge severity and track response
Screening for comorbid depression and alcohol or substance use
Developmental history to distinguish from autism spectrum and personality disorders
redFlags: Emerging suicidal ideation, particularly with comorbid depression
Escalating alcohol or sedative use to cope with social situations
Progressive social isolation with collapse of education, employment, or relationships
reference.prognosis: Social anxiety disorder is often chronic and, if untreated, can persist for many years with substantial functional impairment. Prognosis improves with cognitive behavioural therapy and pharmacotherapy, and is better with earlier onset of treatment and fewer comorbidities; the performance-only subtype generally carries a more favourable outlook.
pitfalls: Dismissing the presentation as mere shyness and missing significant impairment
Overlooking comorbid alcohol misuse used as self-medication
Failing to include exposure-based work, which is central to durable improvement
Prescribing daily benzodiazepines and risking dependence
Stopping SSRIs prematurely before an adequate response has developed
management: Cognitive behavioural therapy with graded exposure and cognitive restructuring as first-line treatment.
Pharmacotherapy with SSRIs or SNRIs as effective first-line agents, with monoamine oxidase inhibitors as a later option in resistant disease.
Beta-adrenergic blockers for the performance-only subtype to control autonomic symptoms of situational anxiety.
Identify and treat comorbid depression and alcohol or substance misuse, avoiding reliance on benzodiazepines.
Track severity and treatment response with standardised social anxiety rating scales and assess suicide risk.
Refer to specialist psychological or psychiatric services for severe, refractory or highly comorbid presentations.
